Get started with bootmakr in Stata

Source: vignettes/articles/stata.Rmd
stata.Rmd

A regression coefficient from observational data is only as credible as the assumption that no important variable was left out. A sensitivity analysis asks how strong an omitted variable would have to be to change the conclusion. sensemakr (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020) answers with a concrete number: the coefficient you would have obtained had a variable as strong as one of your observed covariates been omitted.

bootmakr adds inference to that number that does not rely on the conventional OLS variance formula. It bootstraps the whole procedure, so the standard error, confidence interval and p-value of the adjusted coefficient remain usable when the errors are heteroskedastic or correlated within clusters. This page shows a first analysis from start to finish. The same steps in R are in Get started in R.

Installation

bootmakr builds on the sensemakr command, which is on SSC. bootmakr itself is installed from GitHub.

ssc install sensemakr
net install bootmakr, from("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jespernwulff/bootmakr-stata/main/")

Stata 14 or later is required. To update an existing installation, add the replace option to net install. After installation, help bootmakr opens the help file, which is also on this site.

The example

We use the data of Chen, Chittoor, and Vissa (2021), who ask whether CEOs that belong to the family controlling the firm are paid more than professional CEOs. The authors share their data on OSF. copy downloads the file to the working directory.

global osf "https://osf.io/download/stk7y/?view_only=885d1ed5498c4b3c8a1194882e468286"
copy "$osf" "ceo_pay.dta", replace
use "ceo_pay.dta", clear

The data hold 2,011 firm-year observations of 277 Indian firms. lg_ceopay is the logarithm of total CEO pay, owner_ceo indicates a family CEO, and co_code identifies the firm. We keep the control variables of the published model (CEO tenure and education, firm sales and age, ownership shares, and year and industry indicators) in a global macro.

global controls "ceo_tenure PA_nic3_med ceo_edu_dummy lg_sales firm_age"
global controls "$controls promoters_pct institutions_pct i.year i.nic_code_1digit"
quietly regress lg_ceopay owner_ceo $controls, vce(cluster co_code)
lincom owner_ceo
 ( 1)  owner_ceo = 0

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   lg_ceopay | Coefficient  Std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
         (1) |   .3269285   .1018931     3.21   0.001      .126342    .5275149
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is the published coefficient (Model 2 of their Table 2), with standard errors clustered by firm. Family CEOs earn more.

A first analysis

Could an omitted variable explain this away? To answer, sensemakr needs a benchmark: an observed covariate that sets the scale for the omitted variable. We take the age of the firm and ask what the coefficient of owner_ceo would be had a variable as strong as firm_age been omitted.

bootmakr lg_ceopay owner_ceo $controls, ///
    treat(owner_ceo) benchmark(firm_age) cluster(co_code) seed(123)
Bootstrap results                               Number of obs     =     2,011
                                                Replications      =     1,000

                 (Replications based on 277 clusters in co_code)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |      Observed    Bootstrap                    Percentile
             |       Coef.      Std. Err.    P-value    [95% Conf. Interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
owner_ceo    |    .3031863      .1079588      0.0020     .0919355     .517261
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: CI is percentile bootstrap confidence interval
      P-value is bootstrap p-value (H0: owner_ceo = 0)
      Benchmark: firm_age, kd = 1, ky = 1

Benchmark strength (descriptive; no standard errors involved)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Benchmark: firm_age
                                                 Partial R2    |Partial corr.|
  with owner_ceo | X                                 0.0394             0.198
  with lg_ceopay | owner_ceo, X                      0.0023             0.047
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
     kd      ky      R2dz.x     R2yz.dx    |r_dz.x|   |r_yz.dx|
   1.00    1.00       0.0410     0.0024      0.202      0.049
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: R2dz.x (R2yz.dx) = partial R2 of the omitted variable with the
      treatment given the covariates (with the outcome given treatment
      and covariates). |r| = square root, i.e. the partial-correlation
      scale of the ITCV. Descriptive only: no t-implied correlation or
      threshold is reported.

The command line has the same form as regress: the outcome first, then the treatment and the covariates. The options name the treatment (treat()), the benchmark (benchmark()) and, because observations of the same firm are not independent, the variable that identifies the clusters to resample (cluster()). Everything else is left at its default: an omitted variable exactly as strong as the benchmark (kd(1)) and 1,000 bootstrap replications. seed() makes the result reproducible. The run takes about a minute. For longer runs, dots(100) prints a dot for every 100 replications.

Reading the output

The adjusted estimate. Had a variable as strong as firm_age been omitted, the coefficient of owner_ceo would be 0.303 rather than 0.327. This is the estimate sensemakr reports for the same benchmark. It does not involve the bootstrap.

Its uncertainty. The remaining columns come from the bootstrap. In each of the 1,000 replications bootmakr draws firms with replacement, reruns sensemakr and stores the adjusted estimate. The standard deviation of those 1,000 values is the standard error (0.108), their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles form the 95 percent confidence interval (0.092 to 0.517), and the p-value (.002) is twice the smaller of the two shares of replications that fall on either side of zero. The pay premium of family CEOs remains positive and statistically distinguishable from zero even if an omitted variable as strong as firm age is at work.

The benchmark strength. The second block says what “as strong as firm_age” means: the share of the remaining variance of the treatment and of the outcome that firm age explains (partial R2), the corresponding partial correlations, and the strength of the omitted variable these numbers imply. All of this is computed from the data. No standard error is involved, so the block is the same whatever variance estimator you prefer. See How strong is the benchmark? for the details.

From one strength to many: the breakdown point

An omitted variable as strong as firm age does not overturn the result. How much stronger would it have to be? Give kd() several values and bootmakr evaluates each of them on the same bootstrap samples. The plot option draws the result.

bootmakr lg_ceopay owner_ceo $controls, ///
    treat(owner_ceo) benchmark(firm_age) kd(0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 4) ///
    cluster(co_code) seed(123) plot
Bootstrap results                                Number of obs     =     2,011
                                                 Replications      =     1,000

Adjusted estimate and bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval for an omitted variable 0.5 to 4 times as strong as firm age. Solid markers: p < .05.

The adjusted estimate shrinks as the assumed omitted variable grows stronger, and its confidence interval widens. In this run the result holds up to an omitted variable 2.5 times as strong as firm age and breaks down at 3 times: from there on the interval includes zero. That breakdown point is a compact summary of how robust the finding is.

A p-value close to .05 can fall on either side of it from one seed to the next when only 1,000 replications are drawn. Before reporting a breakdown point, increase reps() and check that the result has settled. The worked example repeats this sweep with 10,000 replications and puts the breakdown point at 2.5.

With several values of kd(), the full table is returned in r(results) and the implied strength of the omitted variable in r(benchmark_strength).

The choices you make

The benchmark. Choose an observed covariate that is strong and that you can argue an omitted variable is unlikely to exceed. Report why you chose it. A group of covariates can serve as a joint benchmark with gbenchmark(x1 x2).

The multiple. kd() scales the benchmark’s relationship with the treatment and ky() its relationship with the outcome. ky() follows kd() unless you set it.

The resampling scheme. It should mirror how the data were sampled and how you would compute standard errors in the regression itself. Without cluster(), observations are resampled, which allows for heteroskedasticity. With cluster(id), whole clusters are resampled, and strata() requests a stratified bootstrap. See Clustered and stratified data.

Replications and seed. The default of 1,000 replications is fine for a first look. For results you report, use more (reps(5000) or reps(10000)), set a seed(), and when the verdict is close to the significance threshold check that it has settled with the converge() option.

Many indicator variables. Stata re-estimates the regression in every replication. A model with hundreds of indicator variables (say, one per village or firm) can take about a second per replication, so start such a model with a few hundred replications and dots() to see how long it will take.

Bootstrapping your own program

In standard mode bootmakr builds the sensemakr call for you. If something has to happen in every replication before sensemakr runs, or you want full control over the call, write a small e-class program and hand it to bootmakr with program(). The program must leave sensemakr’s e(bounds) behind. treat() is then only a label for the output.

capture program drop my_sens
program define my_sens, eclass
    sensemakr lg_ceopay owner_ceo $controls, ///
        treat(owner_ceo) benchmark(firm_age) kd(1) suppress
end

bootmakr, treat(owner_ceo) program(my_sens) cluster(co_code) seed(123)
Bootstrap results                               Number of obs     =     2,011
                                                Replications      =     1,000

                 (Replications based on 277 clusters in co_code)
                 (Using user-supplied program: my_sens)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |      Observed    Bootstrap                    Percentile
             |       Coef.      Std. Err.    P-value    [95% Conf. Interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
owner_ceo    |    .3031863      .1079588      0.0020     .0919355     .517261
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: CI is percentile bootstrap confidence interval
      P-value is bootstrap p-value (H0: owner_ceo = 0)

Benchmark strength (descriptive; no standard errors involved)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
     kd      ky      R2dz.x     R2yz.dx    |r_dz.x|   |r_yz.dx|
   1.00    1.00       0.0410     0.0024      0.202      0.049
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: R2dz.x (R2yz.dx) = partial R2 of the omitted variable with the
      treatment given the covariates (with the outcome given treatment
      and covariates). |r| = square root, i.e. the partial-correlation
      scale of the ITCV. Descriptive only: no t-implied correlation or
      threshold is reported.

With the same seed this reproduces the first analysis exactly. In program mode the benchmark-strength block shows only the implied strength of the omitted variable, because bootmakr does not know which covariate your program uses as benchmark.
